shareValue: A ten-second stress test for high-pressure screens and workflows.
caption:
I kept worrying about what the law actually let me do, and what I was allowed to do if things went wrong. Never had a good answer.

So I built the thing I wanted in my pocket. Seven years later I'm still adding to it.

slides.text: An emergency screen should feel boring.
What law actually protects me here?
slides.kicker: What am I allowed to say? What are they allowed to do? The moment you need the answer is the worst moment to start googling.

slides.text: Design for the moment, not the menu
items: Show the right or next step
Put real help one tap away

slides.text: Nobody opens this out of curiosity.
slides.kicker: Everyone opening it is having a bad day.
Red means emergency. Only emergency. Not errors, not delete buttons, not accents because it looks nice. The app icon isn't red either.

slides.text: Every emergency number is one tap to call.
slides.kicker: A stressed user should not have to copy, remember, or navigate again.

items: Can one tap reach real help?

captions.instagram:
An emergency screen should feel boring.

When someone opens Malaysia Pocket under stress, visual cleverness becomes friction. The hierarchy needs to be obvious, the language calm, and an important number one tap away.

That is why red is reserved for emergencies instead of decoration. Restraint is doing product work. Save the final stress test before reviewing a critical flow.

What would you remove if your user had only ten seconds?
